headline: The audit trail recorded a partial result as a success and scrubbed the fields that say what happened
summary: `warning` was mapped to `success`, so a row describing a partial result read exactly like one with nothing wrong in it, and an outcome the vocabulary did not recognize became `success` too. Separately, the always-redacted field list matched short entries as substrings: `auth` scrubbed `authenticated`, `authservId` and `author`, and `ssn` scrubbed `className`. Both defects removed information from the trail an operator reads after something has gone wrong.

items.title: The WebSocket same-origin default compares the whole origin
items.body:
`b.websocket.isOriginAllowed`'s default compared the `Origin` header's host against the `Host` header. RFC 6454 defines an origin as the triple of scheme, host and port, and neither of those two values carries a scheme, so the check tested one member of three: a page at `http://` the same host passed it. The docstring above it stated that this default closes the cross-site WebSocket hijacking class, and against a network attacker or a mixed-content page at the cleartext origin it did not.

All three members are compared now. The scheme comes from the connection, and the host from the authority the request named, so an HTTP/2 upgrade — which carries no `Host` header at all and was previously refused outright — is compared correctly.

The scheme is resolved the way every other scheme decision in the framework is: from `X-Forwarded-Proto` when the immediate peer satisfies a `trustProxy` predicate, then from the HTTP/2 `:scheme` pseudo-header, then from the connection. `b.requestHelpers.requestProtocol` reads `:scheme` for every caller, which is what an RFC 8441 extended CONNECT needs — its request is built from headers alone and carries no socket to ask. A deployment terminating TLS at a proxy passes that predicate to `b.websocket.handleUpgrade`, which hands it to the check; without it the backend socket is cleartext and an `https` Origin is a cross-scheme request. `isOriginAllowed` takes the same options as a third argument for callers using it directly.

items.title: The origin check reads the authority an HTTP/2 request named
items.body:
Node does not map the HTTP/2 `:authority` into `req.headers.host`, and this framework's TLS listeners advertise `h2` first, so every current browser negotiates HTTP/2 against them and that header is absent. Five places read it alone and reached two opposite failures from the one premise.

`b.middleware.csrfProtect` built its same-origin baseline by concatenating the scheme with that header, so over HTTP/2 the baseline was a bare scheme, every browser `Origin` mismatched, and the gate **refused every form submission**. The same request with the same token returns 302 over HTTP/1.1 and 403 over HTTP/2. `b.middleware.hostAllowlist` read the absence as a malformed request and denied it as `missing-host`. `b.middleware.cors` inferred no origin at all, `b.middleware.botGuard` stopped recognizing loopback as a secure context, and the 0-RTT replay key hashed an empty component for every HTTP/2 request.

`b.requestHelpers.requestHost` now answers with the `:authority` when one is present and the `Host` otherwise, and the five readers go through it.

It prefers the pseudo-header rather than falling back to it, which closes a second problem: `Host` and `Origin` are both caller text, so a non-browser client over HTTP/2 could write both halves of the comparison and have the check agree with it. `:authority` comes from the connection. Not browser-reachable, since `Host` is a forbidden header name, so this was defense-in-depth rather than a live CSRF path.

A trusted `X-Forwarded-Host` still takes precedence over both, and is still ignored from an untrusted peer.

items.title: An unrecognized audit outcome is no longer recorded as a success
items.body:
`b.audit.safeEmit` normalizes the outcome it is given, and anything the vocabulary did not carry became `success`. A caller that wrote `faliure`, or passed a value from a newer vocabulary than the table knew, recorded a successful operation. On a trail that exists to be read after something went wrong, that is the wrong direction to fail in.

`b.audit.record` refuses an unrecognized outcome, as it did before. `safeEmit` cannot: it is drop-silent by contract, and throwing would lose the row it was called to preserve. It now records `failure` instead, so a typo becomes a row somebody investigates rather than one nobody reads.

An OMITTED outcome is unchanged and still records `success`. Leaving the field off is not a misclassification, it is no classification, and several events already emitted that way; turning them into failures would fill the trail with rows describing things that never went wrong.

The normalizer's targets are also held to the vocabulary when the module loads, so the two lists cannot drift into disagreeing: an entry pointing at a value `record` refuses would silently drop every row that used it.

items.title: A refusal reaches the peer before the connection is torn down
items.body:
All five mail listeners ended the connection and destroyed the socket on the next line. `end()` queues the FIN behind whatever is still in the write buffer, and the `destroy()` did not wait for it, so whether a refusal arrived depended on whether it happened to fit in the kernel socket buffer, which depends on how much the peer sent rather than on anything the server decided.

Measured against an MX with a 1 MiB ceiling and an undeclared `DATA` body: 2 KiB over the limit delivered `552 5.3.4`, 64 KiB over delivered it and then a clean FIN, and 256 KiB over delivered nothing at all and reset the connection. The failure ran the wrong way round. A small overshoot, where retrying is cheap, got the permanent answer; a large one, where retrying is expensive for both ends, got the reset. RFC 5321 section 4.2.1 makes that difference load-bearing: a peer that receives a permanent code stops and reports to its sender, and one that receives nothing has no verdict and re-sends for the whole of its queue lifetime. Several refusals on this path are ones a hostile peer can trigger deliberately, so the reply most worth delivering was the one most likely to be lost.

The socket is now destroyed once the reply has flushed, with the socket's own close and a five-second timer as backstops so a peer that stops reading cannot hold the connection. The session is still marked closed immediately, so a queued command is never executed after a refusal. A connection held open to flush stays counted by `connectionCount()` until it actually closes.

items.title: A JMAP blob download does not take its type from the requester
items.body:
`b.mail.server.jmap`'s download endpoint used the request's own `accept` query parameter as the response `Content-Type` whenever the backend reported none, and set `Content-Disposition: attachment` only when a filename was present and matched a narrow pattern. A blob with no filename, or one carrying a space, was served inline.

Together those return bytes under a type the URL chose, rendered inline, from an endpoint that requires an authenticated actor. Where the bytes are attacker-influenced, which is the ordinary case for a mail attachment, `?accept=text/html` is script execution in the application's origin.

RFC 8620 section 6.2 makes `accept` a request. The response type is now what the blob is, or the generic type when the backend reports none, and a type that is not a well-formed media type is not written into the header at all. Every download is an attachment; an unquotable filename costs the name, not the disposition.

Reachable only through a consumer that implements `mailStore.downloadBlob`, which the framework does not ship — such a consumer inherited the behavior with no warning that it had.

items.title: A CSRF origin refusal names its reason
items.body:
`b.middleware.csrfProtect` refuses a request that carries neither `Origin` nor `Referer` when `requireOrigin` is set. That refusal was audited as `origin/referer: [object Object]`, because the check returned an object on that one path where its four other exits return a reason string and the caller builds the line by concatenation.

The gate itself was never weakened: the object is truthy and the caller compares against null, so the request was refused either way. What was lost is the reason, on the one configuration an operator turns on deliberately, and in the trail it was indistinguishable from any other object that might arrive there later.

items.title: An API key's scope is bound to the credential it belongs to
items.body:
The sealed columns on the API-key registry carried no binding to the row they sit on unless a compliance posture was pinned, so a sealed cell could be moved from one credential's row to another's. `ownerId` is the scope: it is what `b.apiKey.verify` returns for an application to decide what a credential may do. Measured by copying one credential's sealed `ownerId` onto a second credential's row: `verify` for the second token returned the first's owner. On a credential registry that makes database write access an escalation rather than a disclosure, and sealing the column was what was supposed to prevent it.

The columns are now bound to `(table, row, column)` on every deployment. The registry is declared by the framework, so this was not something an application could turn on for itself, and a compliance posture is a decision about a whole deployment taken for unrelated reasons.

Upgrade note: rows written by an earlier version carry the unbound form, and a bound column refuses one on read. An unbound cell is precisely what an attacker with write access would place, so accepting one is a hole for as long as it is accepted, and the framework does not ship that open. A deployment with existing API keys opens a window for the length of its migration:

```js
b.db.init({ /* ... */ allowPlainSealMigration: ["_blamejs_api_keys"] });
```

Rows re-seal as bound on their next write, and each read of a still-unbound cell records `system.crypto_field.plain_cell_accepted`. Remove the option once that count reaches zero. A deployment with no existing keys needs nothing.

`b.safeDecompress` also separates two refusals that shared one code: `safe-decompress/output-cap-exceeded` for output past `maxOutputBytes`, and `safe-decompress/decompress-failed` for a stream that is malformed. A caller acts differently on the two, and telling them apart previously meant reading zlib's own wording, which differs across Node releases.

items.title: A sender-policy refusal reaches the client instead of the socket the connection opened on
items.body:
When a composed `senderPolicy` raises, `b.mail.server.submission` refuses the sender, which is the documented fail-closed behavior. The refusal was written to the connection's original socket. The listener requires STARTTLS before it accepts an envelope, so by the time a `MAIL FROM` reaches a sender policy the connection has always been upgraded and that socket is the wrong one: the reply reached nobody and the client waited out the idle timeout.

From the sender's side that is indistinguishable from a dead server, and it is the worst shape a refusal can take, because a client that receives no code cannot classify the failure and re-sends the same message. The refusal now goes to the socket the session is actually on.

An `eslint` rule refuses the shape across all five mail listeners: a handler takes the live socket as a parameter, and a nested function reading the connection's own binding is reported. It asks the scope analyzer which binding a reference resolves to rather than matching the name, so a callback registered on that socket, and a parameter carrying whichever socket is current, are unaffected.

items.title: A DMARC aggregate report is bounded by expansion as well as by size
items.body:
`b.mail.dmarc.parseAggregateReport` capped decompressed size and said nothing about how little input produced it, and the input arrives from anyone who sends a report to a published `rua=` address. It now runs through `b.safeDecompress`, which bounds compressed size, decompressed size and expansion ratio, and records a refusal to the audit trail.

The ratio is set from measurement rather than from the sibling parser's 50:1 default, which would refuse ordinary mail: a generated report reaches 38:1 at 100 records, 63:1 at 1,000 and 109:1 at 10,000, and a report from a single sending host reaches 225:1. The cap sits at 300:1, about three times the largest measured legitimate ratio and about a third of what the gzip format itself can produce. The absolute size cap remains the bound that does the work.

A ZIP-delivered report is named as one instead of failing later as malformed XML. RFC 7489 §7.2.1.1 allows it, and `b.archive.read.zip` reads the entry out; the refusal says so.

Separately, a report of any real size was being refused. The XML parse was given a byte cap and left at the parser's 10,000-element default, and one `<record>` expands to seventeen elements, so a report was refused at about 580 records while the documented record cap is 10,000 — and refused as malformed XML, which names no limit. The element cap is now derived from the record cap.

items.title: The always-redacted field list no longer scrubs by substring on short names
items.body:
Field names are matched case-insensitively and by substring, which is what makes `userPassword` redact under `password`. Six entries are too short for that to mean anything: measured against the field names this framework emits, `auth` matched 93 of them, `sid` 32, `pin` 29, and `ssn` matched `className`.

What was scrubbed is what an operator reads to find out what happened: `authenticated` and `authenticatedAs`, whether a check passed and as whom; `authservId`, the RFC 8601 identifier naming which server wrote an `Authentication-Results` header; `author`, which RFC 5322 section 3.6.2 uses for the `From` party; and, through `sid` and `pin`, `residency`, `sidecar`, `residentKey`, `stepIndex` and `mapping`.

`auth`, `pin`, `sid`, `ssn`, `cvc` and `cvv` are matched as a whole segment of the field name, and as an occurrence at a name boundary so a caller that normalizes its keys to lowercase is covered too: `authcode`, `ssnnumber`, `last4ssn` and `customercvv` are all still redacted, as are the camel forms. Every longer entry keeps substring matching.

What may follow each short name and still be an ordinary word is a closed list, decided from the field names this framework actually emits rather than from the nouns that would make one a secret: enumerating the nouns is open-ended and fails silently on the one nobody listed. `authentication` is readable and `authenticationCode` is a credential, and the two are identical up to the noun, so the exemption is anchored at both ends — a compound that is not on the list is redacted rather than exposed.

items.title: `warning` is an audit outcome
items.body:
It was accepted as a word and mapped to `success`, which is the one thing it cannot mean: `success` and `warning` are the two answers a partial result needs to tell apart. An ingest that stored 490 of 500 records is neither a success nor a denial, and recorded as a success its row is indistinguishable from one that had nothing wrong with it, so the query an operator would run to find partial results returns nothing.

The vocabulary is now `success`, `warning`, `failure`, `denied`, accepted by `b.audit.record` and by `safeEmit`. Advisory and deadline-miss outcomes the framework already emitted — a residency-gate advisory, an incident stage recorded past its deadline — record as `warning` rather than as successes.

Upgrade note: a consumer that queries for `outcome = 'success'` to mean "nothing to look at" now sees fewer rows, which is the point. Rows that previously said `success` because their outcome was unrecognized now say `failure`.

items.title: A message stores every octet the peer sent, whichever way it arrived
items.body:
The `DATA` path stored a message two octets shorter than it was transmitted, because it read the whole `<CRLF>.<CRLF>` terminator as framing. RFC 5321 §4.1.1.4 says the first of those CRLFs "is actually the terminator of the previous line", so it belongs to the mail data, and this framework's own `BDAT` and IMAP `APPEND` paths kept it: two of the four ways a message enters disagreed with the other two.

What that costs is not only two octets. `POP3 RETR` restores a trailing CRLF only when the body lacks one, so a message whose last line is blank still ended with CRLF after the subtraction and the blank line was gone: the account holder received a message one line shorter than the one sent, and a MIME epilogue is made of blank lines. A message with no body lost its header separator entirely, so the stored form contains no `\r\n\r\n` and a DKIM signature over it cannot be evaluated. A consumer storing bodies under a digest got two different blobs for one message depending on which door it came through.

`b.safeSmtp.findDotTerminator` now returns what its own documentation always described, the index where the mail data ends. That index is two octets further on than before, so a caller slicing to it stores what the peer sent. Empty mail data terminates as well: a client answering the 354 with `.\r\n` sends three octets, the CRLF that opens the terminator having ended the `DATA` command line, and the five-byte scan never matched it — the collector waited for a terminator that had already arrived.

`b.safeSmtp.dotStuff` documented a trailing CRLF it does not append. It stuffs and nothing else, and the caller owns the line the terminator needs; the documentation says that now. Both current callers already did it.

DKIM body hashes are unaffected: RFC 6376 §3.4.3 and §3.4.4 each append a CRLF when the body lacks one.

items.title: `GETSCRIPT` closes the literal it announced
items.body:
`b.mail.server.managesieve`'s `GETSCRIPT` announces an octet count, writes the script, and then wrote the CRLF that closes the literal only when the script did not already end with one. A Sieve script ending in CRLF is the ordinary case, so a conforming client read the announced octets and found `OK "GETSCRIPT completed"` where the terminator belongs. RFC 5804 §2.9 puts the CRLF there unconditionally, and the count was already in hand on the line above, so the framing never needed to be inferred from the payload.

A detector refuses the shape: a CRLF written to a socket under a test on what the payload ends with. `b.mail.server.pop3`'s `RETR` is unaffected — it announces no count, so the terminator's leading CRLF has to come from the body or from the server, and it tests the trailing bytes directly.

items.title: A delivery report quotes the headers that were sent
items.body:
`b.mail.send.deliver`'s DSN builder extracted the original header block by decoding the message as UTF-8 first. That decode substitutes U+FFFD for any sequence it cannot read rather than reporting it, and a message off the wire is not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8: a legacy 8-bit header, or a raw byte in an unencoded parameter, survives transmission and did not survive this. The bounce then quoted headers the sender never wrote, which is the part of a delivery report a person reads most closely.

The header block is now located in the message's own bytes. A block that is valid UTF-8 is quoted as before, and the part names the charset, which `text/*` otherwise defaults to US-ASCII. A block that is not valid UTF-8 is carried under `Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64` (RFC 2045 §6.8), so every original octet reaches the reader and the part's label describes the bytes that are actually there.

The block's end was also wrong for one of the two message forms. The separator's own line terminator is two octets when the message uses CRLF and one when it uses bare LF, and a fixed two was added either way, so the same message spelled two ways produced header blocks that differed by more than their line endings. The width is now carried out of the match.

items.title: A DKIM key record with upper-case tag names no longer verifies here
items.body:
RFC 6376 §3.2 interprets tag names case-sensitively. `b.mail.dkim` folded them, so a selector record published as `V=DKIM1; K=rsa; P=<key>` verified here and is refused by every conforming verifier, which finds no `p=` tag and therefore has no public key.

The direction of that is what makes it worth changing: the operator is told their DKIM is correct while the receivers they actually send to treat their mail as unsigned, and nothing on the sending side can see it, because the only party that reports the truth is the receiver. An application checking its own published record against its own key got the lenient answer too.

ARC is the same production by normative import (RFC 8617 §3.8) and had the same behavior; a seal written `I=1` was read as instance 1.

DMARC, BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT are unchanged. None of those specifications states a case rule for tag names, and reading them strictly would refuse a record and yield no policy at all, which is the wrong direction to fail in.

items.title: `app.listen` rejects on a bind failure instead of ending the process
items.body:
`b.createApp(...).listen()` wrapped its bind in a `try`/`catch`, which sees only a synchronous throw. A bind failure arrives asynchronously as an `error` event on the server, and nothing listened for it, so `EADDRINUSE` and `EACCES` ended the process instead of rejecting the returned promise. The port already being taken is the ordinary way an operator meets this, and what they got was a dead process rather than an error they could report.

The returned promise now rejects with the bind error, matching what the framework's mail listeners and `b.testing.listenOnRandomPort` already do. The handler is removed once the bind succeeds, so a later server error is not swallowed.

items.title: A second `MAIL` inside an open transaction says what is wrong
items.body:
`b.mail.server.submission` and `.mx` refused a second `MAIL FROM` with `503 5.5.1 EHLO/HELO first`. The client had already issued EHLO, successfully, so a reader who trusts the reply goes looking for a session that lost it. RFC 5321 section 4.1.4 describes this case as a sender already specified, and that is what the reply now says.

The verdict was always right, so nothing on the wire is newly accepted or refused. The guard that produced it also tested a session stage neither listener ever assigns, so half of its condition could not exclude anything; it now tests whether a sender is set, which is the condition the specification names.

items.title: `Document-Policy` is not sent by default
items.body:
The default named `document-write`, `unsized-media` and `oversized-images`. The last two came out of the Document Policy origin trial and are not in shipping Chrome, `document-write` is not implemented as a document policy either, and Firefox and Safari do not implement `Document-Policy` at all. The header therefore carried no mitigation and logged one `Unrecognized document policy feature name` warning per feature on every navigation, which is how a real warning gets missed later.

The comment beside it claimed the `document-write` feature disabled the legacy DOM-injection API. It did not. What does is the `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` already in the default Content-Security-Policy: under it that sink is guarded and throws.

`documentPolicy` remains available for an operator targeting a browser that gains support, and `documentPolicyReportOnly` is unchanged. An operator relying on the previous default was relying on nothing; anyone who wants the header back passes it explicitly.

items.title: A build-time dependency of the fuzzing harness is refreshed
items.body: `browserslist` moves from 4.28.4 to 4.28.8 in the fuzz harness lockfile, clearing GHSA-73wf-gq98-2v4g and GHSA-c83g-rgw3-j3cx. It is a transitive development dependency, is not part of the published package, and the framework's runtime dependencies remain empty.
